summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH 3 COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid; Nicolò Pianta; Simone Bonizzoni; Piercarlo Mustarelli; Riccardo Ruffo
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes composed of 20 mol kg⁻¹ potassium acetate (CH₃COOK) and varying concentrations of sodium acetate (CH₃COONa). The research addresses the limitations of conventional organic electrolytes and standard aqueous systems by exploring the 'water-in-salt' regime to widen the electrochemical stability window (ESW). Four specific compositions were synthesized and characterized using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), rheology, conductivity measurements, and electrochemical testing. The most promising formulation, containing 7 mol kg⁻¹ sodium acetate (7N20K), exhibited a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and an ESW extending up to 3 V under ideal conditions. This electrolyte was successfully paired with a carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (CLTP) NASICON electrode to demonstrate its viability for sodium-ion batteries. The cell achieved a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, an average charge efficiency of 96% at low currents, and retained 90% of its capacity after 60 cycles. Kinetic analysis revealed a low activation energy for charge transfer (0.12 eV), confirming favorable interface properties. The work provides a fundamental physicochemical understanding of these binary acetate systems, highlighting their potential as safe, low-cost alternatives to fluorinated salts in next-generation batteries.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes composed of 20 mol kg⁻¹ potassium acetate (CH₃COOK) and varying concentrations of sodium acetate (CH₃COONa). The research addresses the limitations of conventional organic electrolytes and standard aqueous systems by exploring the 'water-in-salt' regime to widen the electrochemical stability window (ESW). Four specific compositions were synthesized and characterized using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), rheology, conductivity measurements, and electrochemical testing. The most promising formulation, containing 7 mol kg⁻¹ sodium acetate (7N20K), exhibited a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and an ESW extending up to 3 V under ideal conditions. This electrolyte was successfully paired with a carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (CLTP) NASICON electrode to demonstrate its viability for sodium-ion batteries. The cell achieved a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, an average charge efficiency of 96% at low currents, and retained 90% of its capacity after 60 cycles. Kinetic analysis revealed a low activation energy for charge transfer (0.12 eV), confirming favorable interface properties. The work provides a fundamental physicochemical understanding of these binary acetate systems, highlighting their potential as safe, low-cost alternatives to fluorinated salts in next-generation batteries.

Research Context
Super-concentrated aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety and low cost. Conventional organic electrolytes suffer from safety and cost issues. Aqueous systems are limited by the narrow thermodynamic stability window of water. High concentrations reduce water activity to kinetically extend the stability window. Fluorinated salts like LiTFSI enable wide windows but face toxicity and cost barriers. Cost-effective acetate salts like KAc and NaAc lack sufficient fundamental characterization.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to characterize the physicochemical properties of binary acetate electrolytes. It is hypothesized that increasing NaAc concentration widens the electrochemical stability window. The 7N20K composition is predicted to offer the best compromise between transport and stability. NASICON electrodes are expected to facilitate efficient ion intercalation in this environment. The carbon-coated CLTP anode should enable reversible sodium insertion at specific potentials.

Methodological Details
Electrolytes were prepared by dissolving high-purity salts in Milli-Q water. Four binary solutions were synthesized with constant KAc and varying NaAc. The specific compositions tested were 1N20K, 2.5N20K, 5N20K, and 7N20K. A 1 M NaAc solution was prepared as a diluted reference. The CLTP anode was synthesized via a one-pot sol-gel route. Precursors included ammonium dihydrogen phosphate, titanium alkoxide, lithium acetate, and glucose. The precursor was calcined at 800 °C for 6 hours under argon flux. DSC analysis was performed from -120 °C to 90 °C to determine thermal transitions. Viscosity was measured using a parallel plate rheometer setup. Conductivity was measured via EIS using a dip probe cell with platinum foils. Electrochemical tests were conducted in flooded three-electrode cells under nitrogen flux. A carbon-coated NASICON electrode was used to test battery performance.

Procedures And Architectures
The CLTP synthesis involved dissolving precursors in ethanol and forming a gel. The mixture was stirred at 55 °C before heating to 80 °C to remove ethanol. The dried precursor was ground and calcined in a tubular furnace. XRD analysis used a Rigaku Miniflex 600 with a Cu cathode. SEM imaging was conducted using a Zeiss Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity measurements covered temperatures from 10 °C to 40 °C. Conductivity measurements spanned a range from 5 °C to 70 °C. Electrochemical stability was assessed using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV). Galvanostatic charge-discharge was performed with potential limitation. Current rates were stepped from 0.1 C to 10 C and back to 0.1 C. EIS for kinetics was recorded from 1 kHz to 100 kHz under nitrogen. The CLTP electrode was dip-coated on carbon cloth current collectors. Organic benchmark cells used PVDF binders and Super P carbon black.

Key Results
The glass transition temperature (Tg) increased with higher salt concentration. Samples 1N20K and 2.5N20K remained frozen in the glassy state. Samples 5N20K and 7N20K showed cold crystallization and melting endotherms. The 7N20K composition exhibited a liquidus temperature below room temperature. All compositions followed Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher (VTF) behavior for conductivity. Ionic conductivity decreased as electrolyte concentration increased. The 7N20K solution achieved a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C. Viscosity increased with concentration, classifying them as structure-making salts. The 7N20K electrolyte followed Kohlrausch's law of strong electrolytes. The electrochemical stability window expanded with increasing NaAc concentration. The 7N20K electrolyte showed a stability window up to 3 V in ideal conditions. The CLTP anode preferentially inserted sodium cations despite lower concentration. First cycle anodic capacity in 7N20K was 85 mAh g⁻¹. Charge efficiency was 96% at low current and 99% at high current. Capacity retention after 60 cycles was 90%. The charge transfer activation energy was determined to be 0.12 eV. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was around 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
High salt concentration reduces water activity, suppressing hydrogen evolution. The low liquidus temperature prevents premature cell failure from crystallization. Good conductivity despite high concentration suggests water-salt structure formation. The NASICON structure accommodates ions without affecting crystal lattice. Low activation energy indicates very good kinetic properties of the interface. Aqueous electrolytes improve the diffusion of alkaline ions inside the electrode. These results support the design of alkaline ion batteries using the water-in-salt approach.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study notes that anodic ESW expansion is less significant than cathodic. The LSV procedure may lead to overestimated decomposition limits. The study was conducted in ideal conditions with small surface area electrodes. Viscosity measurements were limited by instrumental constraints in the temperature range.

Claims
Highly concentrated binary acetate electrolytes offer a viable alternative to fluorinated salts for sodium-ion batteries. cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available salts conductivity of 21.2 mS cm -1 at 25°C stability window up to 3 V anodic ESW expansion is not as significant procedure may lead to overestimated decomposition limits design electrode interfaces for alkaline ion rechargeable batteries
The 7N20K composition provides the optimal balance of transport and stability properties. best in terms of a compromise low value of activation energy for the charge transfer process ionic conductivity decreases with increasing the electrolyte concentration preventing premature cell failure caused by salt crystallization

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information files are available free of charge.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A diluted 1 M NaAc solution was used for comparison. Pristine LTP was synthesized without glucose for comparison. Performance in WISE was compared to diluted solution.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 reports the DSC thermograms of the electrolyte solutions. Figure 2a displays the dependence of ionic conductivity on temperature. Figure 5 shows the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) profiles. Figure 7 demonstrates better performance in WISE than diluted solution. Figure 8 shows the impedance spectra of the partially sodiated CLTP electrode.

Three Takeaways
Binary acetate electrolytes enable wide ESW and safe operation. The 7N20K/CLTP interface shows high efficiency and retention. Future work should address practical cell assembly beyond ideal conditions.
